title: ‘Closing Night’ Review: Sarah Paulson and Naomi Watts Are Warring Sisters in Cody Fern’s Deliciously Histrionic Melodrama
description: Toward the end of the deep-feeling, deliciously histrionic drama “Closing Night,” the film shifts tone. The first two acts — a whirlwind of long-def
body:
Toward the end of the deep-feeling, deliciously histrionic drama “Closing Night,” the film shifts tone. The first two acts — a whirlwind of long-deferred confrontations and fiery disclosures — lean on lively dark comedy as a pair of warring sisters explode with decades of rage and resentment. Then the film slows its pace, doubling down on doleful sentimentality as it transitions into a more traditional tearjerker.

	The thrilling turbulence of the film’s start and middle make the total despondency at the end feel a little disappointing. But one can also understand why first-time feature director Cody Fern veered into such melancholic terrain. An Australian actor (“American Horror Story”) who co-wrote the screenplay with Dylan Bostick, Fern is consciously working in a rich tradition of matrilineal melodrama. By zeroing in on fragile and anguished women, he positions his characters in a long lineage of cinematic heroines in extremis.
	

	Here, the emotionally besieged are Sandra (Sarah Paulson) and April (Naomi Watts), middle-aged sisters from Michigan who have been bitterly estranged since they were teenagers. Sandra, who moved to Hollywood at 15, is a renowned actress of stage and screen. April is a hairdresser who never left home, and works at the beauty salon owned by their mercurial mother, Diane (Dianne Wiest). The source of the family’s hostility — which dates to immediately before Sandra decamped — is the film’s first major mystery, although it’s soon clear that it hinges on Theo (Toby Wallace), the son April raised on her own.


	When the film begins, Sandra has extended an olive branch to April and Diane by inviting them to New York to see her perform on Broadway. Diane refuses, but April hesitantly makes the trip, only to learn that Theo — an artistic dilettante who lives in the city with his girlfriend, Lucy (Odessa A’zion) — has been lunching with Sandra behind her back. April receives the news as a betrayal. But Theo, long kept in the dark about his mom and aunt’s rupture, sees the meetings as a chance to get to know the famous relative who was, until then, a stranger.
	

	There is an epic theatrical streak running through this family’s female line: a sense that, even in private moments, they imagine themselves cast under a spotlight. Fern establishes this mode during an early scene at the Broadway show, in which he cuts back and forth between Sandra’s line readings onstage and a furious exchange of stage whispers between April and Theo in the audience. By juxtaposing the spectacle of the play with the fuss in the seats, Fern signals that “Closing Night” is itself an exercise in performance. Sandra may be the only professional actress, but April and Diane are equally dramatic — and if Paulson, Watts and Wiest’s performances seem consequently heightened, that’s by design.

	Sandra’s play is cut short when she collapses onstage, setting in motion a principal storyline that involves a health crisis. It’s only a little implausible that Sandra should receive her life-altering diagnosis while her distant sister happens to be in town; remember, the film is operating according to the dramatic logic of an elevated reality. The diagnosis is cataclysmic, bringing Sandra’s career to an abrupt close. And because the disease attacks her memory, it also lends a new weight to the film’s fixation on old wounds. What’s the relationship between repairing and remembering? Can this sibling damage be forgiven, or must it be forgotten?

	The film’s world is composed of dimly lit spaces dressed in moody hues: oxblood, emerald, indigo. Sandra’s stately Manhattan home might as well be located underground for how dark she keeps the place; the curtains are almost always drawn, suggesting her desire for privacy, her tendency toward isolation. The gloom lifts in one crucial scene, late in the film, in which Sandra and April sit side by side before a bright window. Gazing into the sunlight, they seem to confirm that the forlorn moment is also the film’s brightest one.

	In time, Theo and Lucy, two characters more grounded in realism, recede from the picture, providing space for the hysterical matriarchs to really have at one another. Feverish with feeling, the women scream, wail and sob, each one experiencing her misery multiply in real time as the remaining two look on in disdain. The film wisely allows us to see each character’s side, and the three actresses, contorting their faces and their bodies, are entrancing. The great Wiest, clad in leopard print and lipstick, slurs and spits her lines. Watts transforms into a quivering mound of anxiety. And a stellar Paulson expertly exudes snide arrogance, until Sandra breaks open entirely.
	

	Fern’s images are stylish, but his capacity for mood building is his greatest feat. “Closing Night” is, on its face, a somber film, a story of grudges and trauma buried so deep that it’s exhumed only at the last possible moment. But at its world premiere, the film also had the audience roaring with laughter. The bursts of comedy don’t lighten the mood, but instead sharpen the emotion and clarify the intensity, the way a shrewd joke might at a funeral. Even in its closing moments, when the film’s natural humor gives way to a denouement that can feel labored in its despair, “Closing Night” is a stagy delight, a rush of big, brash emotion that leaves you floored.

title: HBO Max Orders French Medical Drama ‘Rush’ Boarded by ‘ER’ Producer Neal Baer
description: HBO Max is expanding its French originals slate with two new shows, the medical drama “Rush” and police horror-thriller “Bodycam,” both of which wil
body:
HBO Max is expanding its French originals slate with two new shows, the medical drama “Rush” and police horror-thriller “Bodycam,” both of which will start shooting this fall.

	Unveiled Tuesday at the Festival de la Fiction in La Rochelle, the projects follow HBO’s recent French originals, from Marie Monge and Vladimir de Fontenay’s “Privilèges” to Sébastien Marnier’s “Paolo” and “The Seduction,” a prequel to “Dangerous Liaisons” starring Anamaria Vartolomei and Diane Kruger. 
	

	“Rush,” an eight-part, 45-minute medical drama, is set within Paris’ emergency medical service and follows three doctors as they respond to emergencies across the French capital. Neal Baer, the veteran producer and writer whose credits include “ER,” is attached as an associate producer. The series was created and written by Nils-Antoine Sambuc, whose credits include “Belphégor” and “En Thérapie.


	“Bodycam,” meanwhile, is an eight-part, 30-minute thriller blending police drama and horror. The series begins during a police intervention in which two officers shoot an unarmed teenager and decide to conceal what happened from their superiors. But things don’t go as planned when the wounded teenager disappears with one of their body cameras. Officers to launch a manhunt across the city but are quickly faced with a series of strange attacks.  “Bodycam” was created by Timothée Hochet, whose credits include the hit show “Calls,” and Benjamin Adam (“Privilèges”), in collaboration with Mehdi Ouahab.

	Clémentine Bobin, director of original fiction for HBO Max France, said both projects reflect an editorial strategy built around genre storytelling with a strong point of view.
	

	“Since its beginnings, HBO has been built around a simple conviction: the most memorable stories are those that take risks, that seize on narratives and genres to offer a singular perspective on society,” Bobin said. “After ‘Privilèges’ and then ‘Paolo’ this year, we have continued writing that story in France. ‘Rush’ and ‘Bodycam’ are fully part of that approach and that heritage,” she continued. 

	Bobin described the shows as “two ambitious series driven by strong visions” that use genre conventions “to tell something deeply human and contemporary.”

	Earlier this week, HBO Max reached an agreement with French guilds to dedicate part of its mandatory investment in French and European content for documentaries and animation, embracing new French sub-quota rules that Netflix, Amazon and Disney are challenging in court.

schema.headline: HBO Max Orders French Medical Drama ‘Rush’ Boarded by ‘ER’ Producer Neal Baer

title: Walk of Fame Honoree Nia Long on Hollywood, ‘Michael’ and Teasing New ‘Friday’ Movie: Ice Cube Is ‘About to Send Us All a New Script’
description: Long before Nia Long could picture her name pressed into the concrete of Hollywood Boulevard, she was a little girl on a city bus rolling down that
body:
Long before Nia Long could picture her name pressed into the concrete of Hollywood Boulevard, she was a little girl on a city bus rolling down that same street — and her mother was at the wheel. 

	“We used to walk down the block and look at all the stars,” Long recalls. She remembers stopping at Dolly Parton’s star, reading aloud the names she knew, then turning to ask her mother about the ones she didn’t. The memory lands differently now, with Parton’s passing Aug. 25 at 80, days before Long sat down with Variety, and the child who once lingered at her star about to receive one of her own. 
	

	“I came here with very humble beginnings,” Long says. “This star is just as much for me as it is for my mother, because she’s the one who brought us here.” 


	Now the boulevard will partly belong to her too. 

	Long was named to the Hollywood Walk of Fame‘s Class of 2025 in the motion pictures category, and her ceremony is set for September 2026 — a milestone the 55-year-old actress admits she never let herself expect. 

	“I stay under the radar. I just do the work,” she says. “I’m diligent. I have a vision for what I want for my life and for my children and for myself, and I let God take care of the rest, because I don’t want to be caught up in the hype.” 

	For Long, the star is deeper than most people you may have seen receive the honor in recent years, and she grows visibly emotional recounting what it stirs. 

	t’s every girl’s dream, and everything women work hard for,” she shares. “The little girl in me is like, ‘Oh my gosh, we did it!’ And the woman in me is, ‘Take a moment and be proud of yourself.’” 
	

	She returns, repeatedly, to all the strong women who came before her. 

	“This isn’t about me. It is a culmination of generational grit and generational commitment, and I’m so lucky to be the one who, in this whole tribe, gets the star,” she says. “It’s the generations of women who have paved the way for me, who have prayed for me, who have guided me when they’re not even here on this planet anymore.” 

	Long is on Zoom, from her home in Los Angeles and seated at her kitchen counter with the sliding doors behind her, where a custodian is cleaning the deck that coyotes keep fouling. She’s relaxed about the whole ordeal — and if you grew up in a Black and/or Brown community of women, you’ve known someone like Nia Long, the kind of person you want to ask a dozen questions, because you know she gives the best advice. Midway through our interview, Long’s phone rings — it’s her son — and she answers without hesitation, excusing herself politely, tending to him before turning back. The interruption says what the interview keeps circling: everything, for Long, is about family. 

	That refusal to chase the noise has shaped a career spanning four decades. Born in Brooklyn to a first-generation Caribbean American mother from Trinidad, Long and her family landed in South Central Los Angeles via Iowa — a childhood of movement she credits with both her range and her rootedness. The family stayed in California almost by accident: her mother came to the West to be married, called off the wedding, fell for the palm trees and never looked back. 

	Her breakout role came with John Singleton’s “Boyz n the Hood,” the 1991 coming-of-age drama that made Singleton the first Black filmmaker nominated for Best Director and, at 24, the youngest ever. From there came “Love Jones,” “Friday,” “Soul Food,” “The Best Man” and her personal favorite of hers, “Roxanne, Roxanne.” Most recently, she plays Katherine Jackson in “Michael,” the Antoine Fuqua-directed King of Pop biopic that is now the highest-grossing biopic of all time. 



	

					MICHAEL, Nia Long as Katherine Jackson, 2026. ph: Glen Wilson / © Lionsgate / Courtesy Everett Collection
									Glen Wilson / © Lionsgate / Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	Playing the Jackson matriarch — “who I like to say is the queen mother” — was a privilege that reconnected her to her own history. Long met the late Michael Jackson decades ago, through Singleton, and never forgot it. “He said my first and last name, and my shoulders perked up — he’s saying it like I’m somebody,” she recalls. Her interpretation of Katherine holds the ache just beneath the surface — a performance built on restraint, what I’d call an emotional simmer. Her reply: “The simmer is what makes the soup good. You can’t make a good soup if you just hurry up and boil everything.” 
	

	She wanted the queen mother “soft and quiet and there and physically strong but also tender.” 

	If a new generation is rediscovering Long and her contemporaries, she has a theory. The ’90s — its music, its films, its pre-social-media privacy — has become an object of fascination, and Long argues the era can’t be imitated or counterfeited. 

	“Certain things can’t be recycled. You have to go to the original source to get that Jones back that makes you feel so connected,” she says. “Everybody wants a taste of it. So where do you go? You go to the artist.” 

	Still, she reserves a particular tenderness for “Love Jones,” the 1997 romance that underperformed on release and has since become a touchstone for cinephiles, especially within the Black community. “It was ahead of its time for Black people. We bombed at the box office,” she says. The film carried a private meaning, too: her father was a poet, and it opened on his birthday. Playing Nina opposite Larenz Tate — who coincidentally plays Berry Gordy in “Michael” — was, she says, the film that whispered a promise: “I’m onto something. This might work out for me.” 

	Her comedic side hasn’t been as explored as many would have hoped. One of the first films I saw her in was the Whoopi Goldberg and Ted Danson comedy “Made in America,” and those comic roots may not be finished, either. Talking about “Friday” and its most-quoted line — “Bye Felicia!” — Long hinted the franchise will ride again. Her former co-star Ice Cube, she says, is “about to send us all a new script” for the simmering sequel. 

	For all the accolades, Long insists the work was never about fame. “I don’t need to be a movie star. I want to tell stories so someone in that audience can say, ‘I thought I was the only one going through this, and I’m not,’” she asserts. 

	She traces that philosophy to working with Singleton, who cast her when she was “a girl who lived on St. Andrew’s Place in South Central L.A. with my single mother.” “He was the first director who wanted to know who I was,” she says. “Those are the most prolific directors, because they’re looking at the woman, they’re understanding the talent, and they take their ego out of the process.” 
	

	The through-line of Long’s story is the brown-skinned women who showed her it was possible — Diana Ross in “Mahogany” chief among them, alongside Diahann Carroll, Stephanie Mills, Minnie Riperton and Phyllis Hyman. “She was brown. We were the same complexion and they all looked like me.” 

	She reaches, one more time, for Dolly — the star marker that stopped her as a child, and the woman the world just lost. “Like Dolly Parton said, ‘I’ve always known who I am, and I’m going to just always be who I am.’” 

	On the boulevard her mother once drove, the little girl will see her own.

schema.headline: Walk of Fame Honoree Nia Long on Hollywood, ‘Michael’ and Teasing New ‘Friday’ Movie: Ice Cube Is ‘About to Send Us All a New Script’

title: Anant Nag to Receive Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India’s Highest Film Honor
description:
Veteran actor Anant Nag will receive the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India’s highest honor in cinema.

	Nag will receive the award at a ceremony in Keva
body:
Veteran actor Anant Nag will receive the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India’s highest honor in cinema.

	Nag will receive the award at a ceremony in Kevadia, Gujarat, on Sept. 22, the Government of India announced. The award will be presented as part of the 72nd National Film Awards.

	The award – instituted in 1969 in memory of Indian cinema pioneer Dadasaheb Phalke, director of “Raja Harischandra” (1913), India’s first full-length feature, who is considered the father of Indian cinema – is given for outstanding contribution to the growth and development of Indian cinema.
	

	Nag made his acting debut in the Kannada-language film “Sankalpa” (1973 and his Hindi-language debut in “Ankur” (1974). He has appeared in more than 300 films across Kannada, Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam, Tamil and Marathi cinema, with notable television work including “Malgudi Days.” 


	Nag has won five Filmfare Awards and five Karnataka State Best Actor Awards, along with the Karnataka Rajyotsava Award, the Karnataka Sahitya Academy Award and the Karnataka State Lifetime Achievement Award. He also holds an honorary doctorate from Bangalore University (North).

	Beyond acting, Nag served as a member of the Karnataka Legislative Council from 1988 to 1994 and as a member of the Legislative Assembly from 1994 to 1999, during which he held the post of Minister of State for Bangalore City Development. He received the Padma Bhushan, one of India’s highest civilian honors, in 2025.

	Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated Nag in a post on X. “Congratulations to the legendary Anant Nag Ji on being conferred the Dadasaheb Phalke Award,” Modi wrote. “For several decades, his effortless performances, remarkable versatility and brilliance have left a very strong mark on Indian cinema, particularly Kannada cinema. In whichever role he has played, he brought rare depth and authenticity. This is indeed a richly deserved honor for a truly distinguished artist.”
	

	Past winners of the Dadasaheb Phalke award include filmmakers Satyajit Ray, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Mrinal Sen, Shyam Benegal and Tapan Sinha, actors Mohanlal, Soumitra Chatterjee, Waheeda Rehman, Amitabh Bachchan, Dilip Kumar, Rajkumar, Sivaji Ganesan, Akkineni Nageswara Rao, Shashi Kapoor, Asha Parekh and Rajinikanth and musicians Manna Dey, Bhupen Hazarika, Lata Mangeshkar and Asha Bhonsle.

schema.headline: Anant Nag to Receive Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India’s Highest Film Honor

body:
Sep 16, 2026 7:56am PT	
	

			


			
			
	

	

		
	
				
	Since 2015, YouTube Music’s Foundry program has had one clear mission: to support the diverse and innovative voices of the global independent music community. We’re proud to have worked with more than 250 artists, helping them build sustainable careers on their own terms. Artists selected for Foundry receive a grant, dedicated partner support from YouTube, access to the latest products and bespoke on and off-platform opportunities.

	Today, we’re welcoming 16 new artists from eight different countries. Meet the latest cutting-edge artists to join the Foundry Class of 2026:
	


Aiobahn (JP), a producer rooted in electronic dance music, bridges Japanese subculture and pop, crafting a distinctive sound all his own.
Asfar Shamsi (FR), a trailblazing force in the French scene, redefining post-rap pop with her raw, honest songwriting and an eclectic sound that effortlessly bridges rap, electronic, and classic pop.
Baran Kok (DE), a boundary-breaking phenomenon in German rap, shaking up the scene with his viral, taboo-free storytelling and uncompromising, high-energy sound.
FLVCKKA (MX) is a pioneering Mexican artist from Chihuahua, redefining the alternative trap scene through her “hypercorridos” style and the creative, genre-blending Neobuchonismo collective, known for distinct visual aesthetics.
Gabriel Jacoby (US), a rising talent crafting intimate, soulful R&B and funk marked by velvety melodies, vulnerable lyricism and multi-faceted musicianship.
harha (JP) is a Japanese unit founded in 2022, composed of harha, a music producer, and yonabe, a female vocalist with a strong and clear voice. To remember the pure thoughts that fade as we grow older, they are expressing emotions through music nurtured by hip-hop.
Jonny Mahoro (DE), a defining force in German indie-pop, captivating fans with his signature blend of poetic intimacy and driving, R&B-infused beats.
José Jr (BR), a multi-instrumentalist singer-songwriter blending folk, rock and traditional Brazilian music to build poetic bridges between daily life and spirituality.
KEVIS Y MAYYKI (MX), a groundbreaking Mexican rap duo from Nuevo León, blend old-school sounds with alternative rock. Their acclaimed 2025 debut, LOS CHICOS DEL NORTE, and recent hits redefine the genre.
Mariasss (BR), a pop sister trio, and Foundry Rising 2025 alums, fuse beautiful vocal harmonies with pop, K-pop and electronic beats in a rich audiovisual universe.
Max McNown (US), a breakout folk-country singer-songwriter known for raw, emotive acoustic storytelling and heartfelt, viral ballads.
Takase Toya (JP), a singer-songwriter/producer handling everything from writing and composing to track-making. His signature track “Doushite feat. Emi Noda” surpassed 1.2 billion cumulative streams, commanding massive popularity across Asia.
This is Lorelei (US), a solo venture from Water From Your Eyes’ Nate Amos whose lo-fi alt-pop is adored by Hayley Williams and indie contemporaries.
Underscores (US), a genre-bending innovator fusing hyperpop with sharp, cinematic conceptual songwriting and world-building visuals.
Yapi (ES), Madrid-born artist who blends Spanish and French lyrics with Afrobeat, blazing a trail for Afro-fusion across Europe and Latam.
Zeina (LB, EG), a Brooklyn-born, Montreal-raised Lebanese-Egyptian artist redefining global pop for a new generation. Blending Arabic, English and French, she has earned two JUNO Award nominations, a Billboard Canadian Hot 100 entry, and a growing international presence.

title: Metallica Announce 2027 North American Tour Dates
description: Metallica has confirmed a series of new North American stadium dates that extend the band’s M72 World Tour into 2027. Having played 99 shows in 26 c
body:
Metallica has confirmed a series of new North American stadium dates that extend the band’s M72 World Tour into 2027. Having played 99 shows in 26 countries since its April 2023 kick-off, the Live Nation-promoted tour will resume May 8, 2027 at BC Place in Vancouver – hitting a dozen new cities for the first time on this run throughout the American southwest, midwest and beyond – and will conclude June 19, 2027 at Rice-Eccles Stadium in Salt Lake City. Support on all dates will be Limp Bizkit and Avatar. See below for a full list of dates.
	

	Tickets for the newly announced shows will be available starting with the Fan Club presales beginning on Monday, September 21 at 10am local time. Additional presales will run throughout the week ahead of the general onsale beginning Friday, September 25 at 10am local time.


	Citi is the official card of the M72 World Tour. Citi cardmembers will have access to presale tickets beginning September 22 at 10am local time until September 24 at 10pm local time through the Citi Entertainment program. For complete presale details visit http://www.citientertainment.com

	Verizon will offer customers an exclusive presale for the newly added M72 shows in the U.S. as part of Verizon’s loyalty program, Verizon Shine. The presale for select shows runs from September 22 at 10am local time to September 24 at 10pm local time. Verizon Shine awards customers with once-in-a-lifetime experiences, alongside daily drops including tickets to concerts and sporting events, exclusive merchandise, dining vouchers, gift cards and more. Opt-in to Verizon Shine via the My Verizon App, and learn more about Verizon Shine here.

title: ‘The View’ Season 30 Launches With Best Premiere Week Ratings in Six Years (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Viewers are still taking a little time to enjoy ABC’s “The View.” The daytime talker, which has been in the crosshairs of the Trump Administration’s
body:
Viewers are still taking a little time to enjoy ABC’s “The View.” The daytime talker, which has been in the crosshairs of the Trump Administration’s FCC, averaged 2.518 million total viewers when it returned for Season 30 last week — up 8% from last year’s audience (2.324 million) and posting the show’s largest overall premiere week audience in six years (since the 2020-2021 TV season).

	“The View” also attracted its best premiere week ratings in four years among women 18-49 and in three years with women 25-54. Also, week 1 of the show’s landmark Season 30 averaged 208,000 women 25-54 (up 7% from 174,000 last year) and 173,000 with women 18-49 (up 15% from 151,000 last year) for the week of Sept. 7, 2026, based on Live + Same Day, Big Data + Panel Data from Nielsen Media Research.
	

	As for the show’s premiere day ratings on Tuesday, Sept. 8, “The View” averaged 2.607 million viewers (up from 2.602 million on Sept. 8 last year), which is also its most-watched season premiere episode in six years (since Sept. 8, 2020).


	The new season opened with a recap of the show’s hiatus (dubbed “Let’s Re-View” day), followed by guests Ted Cruz and Lizzo on Wednesday, Sept. 9; Sherri Shepherd on Thursday, Sept. 10; and Maisie Williams on Friday, Sept. 11.

	Whoopi Goldberg, Joy Behar, Sunny Hostin, Sara Haines, Alyssa Farah Griffin and Ana Navarro are back as hosts on “The View.” The series is executive produced by Brian Teta and is directed by Sarah de la O. There’s also “The Weekend View,” overseen by executive broadcast producer Robin Hommel.
	

	This week’s guests include Colin Kaepernick (“The Perilous Fight”), Neil deGrasse Tyson (“Lost in Space: 5,000 Facts for Navigating the Universe”), Ke Huy Quan (“Never Say Die: A Memoir”), Ethan Hawke (“The Weight”), Clay Aiken (“Rewind”) and Kenny Chesney (“Silver Sands Marina”).

title: Ex-‘Bachelor’ Host Chris Harrison’s Next Dating Show ‘The Vow’ Sets November Premiere on Fox Nation
description: “Roses fade. True love lasts forever,” says Chris Harrison in a cheeky teaser for “The Vow,” his return to reality television five years after his c
body:
“Roses fade. True love lasts forever,” says Chris Harrison in a cheeky teaser for “The Vow,” his return to reality television five years after his controversial exit from the “Bachelor” franchise.

	The new dating show premieres on Fox Nation on Nov. 11, with six episodes rolling out weekly until a series finale on Dec. 9. “The Vow” follows one eligible bachelor, 30-year-old Jace Cates, as he embarks on a “relationship journey” with 10 women looking for lasting commitment and marriage. 
	

	Per the description, the show will explore “whether shared values, faith, communication, and long-term goals can build a relationship designed to last long after the cameras stop rolling. At a time when much of modern dating culture is driven by fleeting connections and social media attention, the series offers a different approach by placing the focus on meaningful relationships, commitment and building a life together.”



	

					Jace Cates, the eligible bachelor of “The Vow”
									Courtesy of Fox Nation
	



	The teaser for “The Vow” did not hold back on drawing the connection between Harrison and TV’s most iconic dating show. The host even throws a red rose — the symbol of “The Bachelor” — on the ground before threatening to step on it.

	And “The Vow” will even feature an appearance from Sean and Catherine Lowe, whose love story unfolded on Season 17 of “The Bachelor” in 2013. The pair has been married since and is one of the most famous examples of a long-lasting relationship to form on reality television. 

	Other “Bachelor” alumni are on board as well, including executive producer Louis Caric, consulting producer Elan Gale as casting director Lindsay Liles and director Michael Shea. Executive producers also include Harrison’s wife, Lauren Zima, plus Lionsgate Alternative Television executives Nicholas Caprio and Tom Huffman.
	

	Harrison hosted “The Bachelor” and all of its spinoffs from the series’ inception in 2002. He exited the franchise in 2021 after comments he made defending former contestant Rachael Kirkconnell drew sharp backlash and were perceived by some as racially insensitive. Kirkconnell was under fire after photos circulated online of her attending an antebellum plantation-themed party as a college student. Harrison apologized for his comments and stepped away from the “Bachelor” franchise temporarily, but Variety reported at the time that Harrison’s team became outraged with the “dragging-out process” surrounding his return “and was unhappy with the network and studio not publicly supporting Harrison.” So, the host negotiated an exit package and largely disappeared from the small screen in the following years.

	“I’m so excited to be back helping people find love, and Fox Nation has been an incredible partner in bringing this vision to life,” Harrison said in a statement. “We were inspired by the faith-driven renaissance happening across America, and as a result, I believe we’ve created the most authentic dating show on television today. At a time when so many people feel dating has become harder than ever, ‘The Vow’ asks a simple but important question: Can genuine, lasting love still be found in the modern world? The stakes couldn’t be higher. I’m incredibly proud and honored to put my name on this show.”

	Fox Nation president Lauren Petterson added, “Chris Harrison helped shape one of television’s most recognizable genres, and we’re thrilled to partner with him on a fresh, thoughtful take that returns the focus to what so many people are ultimately searching for: a genuine connection built to last. This series explores the conversations, values and real-life moments that matter long after production ends, and we believe audiences will connect with its authentic and hopeful approach to finding lasting love.”

	Watch the teaser for “The Vow” below.

title: Tom Petty’s Original Heartbreakers to Reunite for First Time in Decades for Americana Awards, Fronted by Chris Stapleton; Boxed Set of ’70s Rarities Coming
description: It’s almost enough to un-break your heart, if you’re a Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers fan. The four members of the original/classic lineup of Petty
body:
It’s almost enough to un-break your heart, if you’re a Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers fan. The four members of the original/classic lineup of Petty’s longtime band will reunite on stage for the first time in more than 20 years this week, fronted by Chris Stapleton for an opening performance at Wednesday night’s Americana Honors & Awards show in Nashville. That’s happening in conjunction with the announcement of a boxed set due in November that will delve into unreleased material from the group’s earliest days, “Origins 1971-1978.”
	

	The performance on the Americana Awards will have Stapleton backed by Mike Campbell, Benmont Tench, Stan Lynch and Ron Blair. For the finale of the program several hours later, the four OGs will be joined by two latter-day Heartbreakers, Steve Ferrone and Scott Thurston.


	Heartbreakers fans don’t have to experience too much FOMO about missing the on-stage reunion: The Americana Awards will be streamed live via video and audio through several outlets, beginning at 7:30 p.m. ET/4:30 PT. It can be seen on NPR Music’s YouTube channel and the Americana Music Association‘s Facebook page; the audio feed can be found on SiriusXM’s Outlaw Country channel and clear-channel WSM-AM as well as Nashville’s FM stations WRLT and WMOT.

	An additional appearance by the four original Heartbreakers will take place as part of the AmericanaFest Thursday morning, as Tench, Campbell, Blair and Lynch will take part in a panel, “Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers: 50 Years.” (The panel will not be livestreamed.)

	Campbell and Tench were lifers in Petty’s band until the frontman’s 2017 death. Bassist Ron Blair quit the Heartbreakers in 1982, but rejoined 20 years later. Drummer Stan Lynch left the group for good in 1994, seemingly with some musical estrangement from Petty at the time, though he was known to stay in loving contact with other members of the band in subsequent decades. Those four players did subsequently reunite with Petty on stage as a unit once after Lynch’s departure, playing two songs at their Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction in 2002.
	

	For fans who aren’t in Nashville or can’t tune in, the key news will be the Petty estate and UMe announcing the trove of buried treasure in “Origins 1971-1978,” which comes out to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the band on Nov. 6.



	

	



	The set is being previewed as of Wednesday’s announcement with a previously unheard Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers track, “Parade of Loons,” from 1978. A music video has also been released for the track, directed by Peter Sluszka and starring Iain Armitage (“Young Sheldon”); watch it below.



	The boxed set will come in three configurations — a 5-LP edition, a 4-CD set and what is described as an “uber deluxe edition,” each with a Blu-ray and DVD in addition to the audio content. The vinyl will feature an 88-page “fanzine” with liner notes by veteran rock scribes David Fricke and Bud Scoppa, track-by-track annotations from the original band members and archival photos and memorabilia.



	Anyone not able to spring for the boxed set can still look forward to one component being broken out as a single-disc release: “No Sleep Til L.A.” will be available as a stand-alone LP, CD and limited-edition Zoetrope vinyl. The announcement describes it as “a 12-track document of Tom Petty becoming Tom Petty,” exploring the years between the formation of the pre-Heartbreakers band Mudcrutch (which also included Tench and Campbell) and the coming together of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers as the singer-songwriter’s ultimate band. Seven of the 12 tracks are previously unreleased.

	The boxed set also includes remixed and remastered editions of the band’s first two albums, the self-titled and “You’re Gonna Get It,” with extended versions of 11 tracks, including “American Girl” and “Breakdown.”

	Rounding the set out are: “Live from the Record Plant 1977,” released in its entirety for the first time; “The Cut Out Bin,” consisting of five “solo” Petty tracks as he explored working with different musicians prior to the Heartbreakers’ lineup solidifying, including an appearance by Leon Russell; and the band’s 1978 performance on the BBC’s “The Old Grey Whistle Test,” with restored audio at the hands of Ryan Ulyate.
	

	The “Old Grey Whistle Test” performance is the set’s DVD component. The Blu-ray disc has all 51 songs in high-res stereo, Atmos and 5.1 immersive mixes.

title: ‘Run Hide Fight: Infidels’ Review: Jonathan Majors Scrapes the Barrel in This Islamophobic Drivel
description: More an epic act of trolling than a sincere creative endeavor, “Run Hide Fight: Infidels” aspires to “own the libs” and antagonize Muslims, but the
body:
More an epic act of trolling than a sincere creative endeavor, “Run Hide Fight: Infidels” aspires to “own the libs” and antagonize Muslims, but the filmmaking is so shoddy that neither group will likely seek it out, even to assess whether they should be offended. Written and directed by onetime Hollywood hopeful Kyle Rankin (“The Battle of Shaker Heights”), this standalone sequel to his 2020 film “Run Hide Fight” actively parrots the views of its distributor, right-wing media platform The Daily Wire, with its story of a military veteran battling jihadists on a college campus. Yet its comically reductive treatment of characters, regardless of their partisanship, ensures that the film’s transgressions are largely artistic instead of political, rendering it (mostly) unworthy of the outrage its Islamophobic promotional campaign has thus far attempted to stoke.
	

	Following in the footsteps of “Citizen Vigilante” star and fellow embattled actor Armie Hammer, Jonathan Majors fights personal financial insolvency as Clay Saunders, a Delta Force captain whose fellow soldier gets killed while the two of them are apprehending Isis mastermind Asad al-Madhi (Alec Rayme). Seven years later, Saunders embarks on a tour for his new book “America Unafraid,” which aims to detail “the ways Islam will conquer the west.” He arrives at Laughton University for a promotional appearance on the same day that campus protestors, fueled by the encouragement of a mysterious group of “elite freedom fighters,” decide to take over the student union. What the protestors don’t know is that the freedom fighters are actually Islamic terrorists led by Ibrahim (Stephen Hailo), al-Madhi’s son.
	

	Piggybacking on the scrappy disruption of the protestors, Ibrahim’s well-trained foot soldiers fortify themselves at key positions across campus and begin killing students, faculty and the influx of citizens visiting campus for the school’s fall carnival. Ibrahim’s plan is to establish a new caliphate at Laughton, where he will either convert, “purify” or purge the remainder of the Americans his solders have captured.

	Outside the student union, Devlin (JC Kilcoyne), the son of Saunders’ late comrade, decides to take the law into his own hands, albeit primarily to rescue his buddy Kwan (Chris K. Lee), and crush Lizzy (Tyler Aser), who becomes a bargaining chip for Ibrahim after the terrorist discovers that she’s the daughter of a billionaire. Teaming up with Terrence (David Lucas), a quick-witted campus security guard, and his xenophobic roommate P.J. (James Bingham), the heretofore apolitical Devlin attempts both to mount a rescue mission and exact revenge against the school’s violent oppressors, as he begins to learn firsthand about the threats — both existential and violently real — that his late father was fighting to defeat.

	Movies have taken aim at “wokeness” at an increasing pace in recent years, but making fun of political correctness is hardly a new concept; “P.C.U.,” which took its namesake when the concept was still freshly being articulated in the mainstream, came out in 1994. Given its nonstop barrage of zeitgeist-pilfering broadsides against progressivism, “Run Hide Fight: Infidels” practically qualifies as the Jason Friedberg and Aaron Seltzer version of such a send-up. (File it alongside “Date Movie” and “Epic Movie” and retitle it “Liberal Movie.”) Every single character arrives on screen with a fully-baked backstory that amplifies their identity with a stereotype — Kwan, a computer whiz; purple-haired campus revolutionary Farrah (Charlotte Delaney Riggs), an “I like everyone” bisexual — and Rankin coaches them to deliver their expository declarations with comically smug entitlement. If only the movie were trying to be funny.

	Laughton University (actually South Carolina’s Limestone University, if you were curious what venerated institution would allow this film to be shot on their campus) is paralyzed at every level by self-righteous compassion: George (Jason Gray-Stanford), the school’s dean, is too afraid of appearing discriminatory (much less of endorsing law enforcement) to call in the police, and even local mayor Flores (Shazia Pascal) insists upon efforts to “lower the temperature” at the bloody crime scene rather than making a decisive show of force. When a Black professor suggests that the protesting students are infringing on their classmates’ right to use shared areas, her white counterparts shake their heads in disgust for her refusal to capitulate to progressive groupthink.
	

	Rather than making a satirical point about liberal overreach, the movie argues that all this empathy for other people — including for the Indigenous tribes whose land was seized on behalf of the school, or Palestinians trying to hold onto theirs — is a purely oppressive force. Further, it’s in direct opposition to the uncomplicated, common-sense decisions made by men like Saunders who have faced America’s real enemies.

	Unsurprisingly, Rankin’s depiction of Muslims is deeply Islamophobic, although Sue Obeidi, senior vice president for the Muslim Public Affairs Council Hollywood Bureau, has rightly called the film “more ridiculous than it is offensive.” The whole movie is like that — not smart enough to actually explore the viewpoints or value systems of either Muslims or liberals, much less where they come from. Instead, the filmmaker becomes a megaphone for his producer, right-wing commentator Ben Shapiro, whose debate style tends to involve steamrolling his opponent with strawman arguments and acting surprised when they become exasperated. 

	P.J., one of the film’s lead characters, is a foul-mouthed gamer who lies about his military record to justify calling his Egyptian classmate a “camel jockey,” but after a passing callout by Devlin for “stolen valor,” his aspirations to heroism are validated when he ruefully defies local authorities, gridlocked by legal and ethical restraint, to help save the day.

	Majors appears mostly at the beginning and end of the film, giving a thoroughly disengaged performance. (We’re a long way from the awards buzz that his role in “Magazine Dreams” generated at one point.) Then again, the kind of fearmongering peddled here requires a level of conviction that it’s hard to imagine he possesses. The Daily Wire is a perfect platform for “Run Hide Fight: Infidels,” giving it just the right context to set audience expectations. Are you contemptuous of radical leftists who believe that others should be treated with decency, care and respect? If so, this is the film for you. Otherwise, there are dozens of much safer spaces to occupy, whether you’re a bleeding-heart liberal or just a moviegoer with even slightly discriminating tastes.

            The actress wrote a piece for the magazine, published Wednesday, titled "Lena Dunham Is a Mother! The Sweet, Singular Story of How She Prepared."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Heck of an announcement post ... which includes a pic featuring Lena, her husband Luis Felber and their little one.
      

            The pair welcomed their new baby via a surrogate because of Lena's documented history of reproductive challenges.
      
    
            Back in 2017, Lena underwent a hysterectomy -- a surgery to remove the uterus -- due to severe endometriosis. According to the Mayo Clinic, endometriosis is a condition which causes "cells similar to the lining of the uterus, or endometrium, grow outside the uterus."
      
    
            Lena and Luis started dating in 2021 ... and married just months after getting together. Lena revealed to The Times last year that the pair were in the process of expanding their family.
      
    
            Congrats, you two!

            NBC4 Los Angeles started Wednesday morning with heartbreak ... mourning two of its own after the deadly NewsChopper 4 crash.
      
    
            The station opened its 4 AM newscast with an emotional tribute to reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, who were killed Tuesday while on assignment.
      
    
            The anchors told viewers the NBC4 family was grieving, before sharing memories of both colleagues and thanking them for their years of service.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Adrian Arambulo remembered Moreno for the passion and enthusiasm she brought to the job ... saying every time viewers heard her voice from NewsChopper 4, she was "gung-ho" and clearly loved what she did.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Another colleague, who said she'd worked with Moreno since 2014, described her as kind, hardworking, and always on top of things ... while Marciniw was remembered as a deeply respected pilot whose name had become synonymous with NewsChopper 4.
      
    
            The tribute ended with condolences for their families, friends and colleagues ... with the anchors saying Moreno and Marciniw dedicated their lives to helping inform people across Southern California.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Moreno and Marciniw were aboard the helicopter Tuesday evening when it crashed in Chatsworth while they were covering a deadly Metro bus crash. A third person on the ground was also killed.
      
    
            NBC4 anchors were visibly emotional on-air Tuesday night as news of the crash unfolded and the station confirmed the aircraft belonged to NBC Los Angeles.
